Decoding in Order-Agnostic Language Models: Chain-Rule Deviation and Uniform Spreading

Lin Yao Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, 200240, China Affiliation: Zhongguancun Academy, Beijing, 100097, China Email: lin.yao@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

Order-agnostic language models (OALMs), including discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs), are trained to predict masked tokens under arbitrary conditioning sets, allowing sequences to be generated or scored under arbitrary reveal orders at inference time. In LLaDA-2.1, we report three findings. First, the learned conditionals are not exact factorizations of a coherent joint distribution: changing only the reveal order shifts target log-likelihood by up to 0.490.49 nats/token, so likelihood alone mixes content difficulty with path-dependent artifacts. Second, although confidence-first (CF) decoding is order-agnostic, its reveal orders are close to left-to-right (L2R) on content tokens. Third, we propose a complementary diagnostic based on the shape of the confidence trace. A uniform-spreading theorem shows that, at fixed total likelihood, target recoverability is maximized when per-step confidence is spread uniformly; the resulting deviation motivates Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) as a diagnostic for comparing decoding paths. Across C4 and four downstream benchmarks, low variance separates structured paths from random ordering, and variance is consistently associated with downstream correctness. These results support reporting mean confidence and confidence variance jointly when comparing OALM decoding paths.

1 Introduction

We use order-agnostic language models (OALMs) to denote a broad class of language models trained to predict tokens under flexible conditioning patterns, thereby supporting arbitrary inference orders. This class spans NADE-style order-agnostic models (23), permutation language modeling (29), arbitrary-order autoregressive models (9), and recent discrete diffusion language models. In the dLLM branch, models such as MDLM (20) and LLaDA (15) are trained with random masks at varying mask ratios, so a single trained network pθp_{\theta} can infer in any reveal order. This makes dLLMs a natural testbed for isolating reveal-order effects: we can hold the model and prompt fixed while varying only the order, instantiated by representative strategies such as left-to-right (L2R), right-to-left, random, and confidence-first (CF) variants including Max-prob and Top-margin (7, 5). The most direct way to compare orders is to score the same target sequence 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} along each path. At step tt, let Rt−1R_{t-1} be the tokens already revealed by order π\pi, and define qt​(π)=pθ​(xπ⁡(t)∗∣Rt−1,c)q_{t}(\pi)=p_{\theta}(x^{*}_{\pi(t)}\mid R_{t-1},c). One might then compare orders by the summed score ∑tlog⁡qt​(π)\sum_{t}\log q_{t}(\pi). If the model’s conditionals were consistent with a coherent joint distribution, the chain rule would make this sum independent of π\pi. In our fixed-sequence evaluation on LLaDA-2.1-mini, it is not: on 1,0001{,}000 randomly selected C4 (19) examples, each split into a prefix and a target continuation (Fig. 1), the choice of reveal order shifts log⁡P/n\log P/n by up to 0.490.49 nats per token. At this magnitude, the conditional predictions should not be interpreted as different exact factorizations of one joint distribution. Total log-probability is therefore not order-invariant at the scale needed for strategy comparison: it mixes content confidence with ordering artifacts and is insufficient as a standalone quality signal.

To address this, we identify a complementary diagnostic axis. Even when the chain rule pins ∏tqt=P\prod_{t}q_{t}=P regardless of the reveal order π\pi, PP is not the quantity greedy decoding achieves in practice. Instead, recovering the target sequence becomes an allocation problem: at each step, the decoder commits to an argmax over the vocabulary, and success depends not only on the isolated confidence qt=pθ​(xπ⁡(t)∗∣Rt−1)q_{t}=p_{\theta}(x^{*}_{\pi(t)}\mid R_{t-1}), but on how decisively the target wins against its local competitors. Although the reveal order does not change the model parameters, it determines which contexts Rt−1R_{t-1} are encountered, and thus how the total budget PP is allocated across tokens to maintain a winning margin. This sensitivity to the allocation shape arises because greedy decoding acts as a chain of local decisions: a single bottleneck step—where the allocated qtq_{t} is insufficient to secure the argmax—can determine whether the path succeeds, regardless of how high the probabilities are at other steps. Consequently, a path with nn moderately confident steps can be more reliable than one that is highly confident overall but contains a single low-confidence bottleneck. We formalize this through the uniform-spreading theorem (Theorem 3.1), proving that at a fixed total PP, target recoverability is uniquely maximized when confidence is spread uniformly (qt=P1/nq_{t}=P^{1/n}), with the structural cost of non-uniformity captured by Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}). Thus, log⁡P\log P and Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) define two complementary diagnostic axes: the former measures the model’s total budget, while the latter captures the efficiency of the chosen reveal order.

Empirically, the variance axis explains both strategy-level and downstream patterns. On C4 generation, structured one-token-per-step strategies (Forced-AR, Max-prob, and Top-margin) have similar external perplexity but substantially lower Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) than Random. Their similarity has a path-level explanation: the non-EOS reveal orders of Max-prob and Top-margin closely match L2R (§4.3), so the structured strategies trace near-identical content paths, while short-answer prompts additionally induce a tail-EOS cascade under confidence-first rules. On downstream benchmarks (HellaSwag, CMath, MMLU-Pro, IFEval), lower-variance confidence traces are consistently associated with correct generations (§4.4).

Contributions.

  • •

    We document that the model is not a coherent joint distribution. On LLaDA-2.1-mini, log⁡P/n\log P/n of a fixed target spans ∼0.5\sim 0.5 nats/token across reveal orders, exceeding numerical tolerance and revealing that the learned conditionals are not mutually consistent factorizations of a single joint distribution (§4.2).

  • •

    We characterize why CF reveal orders are close to L2R. Reveal-order analysis shows that confidence-first strategies (Max-prob and Top-margin) traverse near-identical content reveal paths to strict left-to-right decoding. The main departure is on short-answer prompts, where confidence-first rules additionally trigger a tail-EOS cascade that Forced-AR cannot exploit (§4.3).

  • •

    We report variance as a supplementary diagnostic for performance reliability. A uniform-spreading theorem (Theorem 3.1) shows that, at fixed total PP, target recoverability is uniquely maximized at uniform qtq_{t} with deviation governed by Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}), identifying Var\mathrm{Var} as an order-dependent diagnostic that complements log⁡P\log P. On four downstream benchmarks, variance is consistently associated with correctness, ruling out an explanation based only on the poor aggregate performance of Random (§4.4).

2 Related Work

Order-agnostic and discrete diffusion language models.

Order-agnostic generative models date back to NADE-style training (23); the family includes XLNet (29) and ARDM (9), as well as the discrete-diffusion branch: MDLM (20), SEDD (14), and LLaDA (15, 4, 3). These works focus on training distributions that support flexible conditioning patterns. We take such a trained OALM, instantiated by a dLLM in our experiments, as given and study the inference paths it induces.

Decoding strategies for masked / diffusion LMs.

A growing literature explores decoding heuristics for OALMs and dLLMs: confidence-based unmasking (7, 5), block-AR schedules, RCR-style remasking and rate control (24), denoising-entropy controls (6), and search over token orders (21, 1). More recent work studies information-gain criteria for choosing the next position (28). Closest in spirit are information-theoretic analyses of generation order and parallel decoding in masked diffusion models (31). These works primarily ask how to choose or improve an order, or how parallel factorization changes the sampling problem; we ask how to interpret the confidence trace produced by an order.

AR vs. non-AR decoders.

The longstanding question of how non-AR decoders compare to AR has been addressed empirically in many domains, with non-AR translation as a canonical case (8). Recent work has also examined fundamental limits and trade-offs of diffusion language models (32) and the ability of any-order architectures to subsume AR as a special case (10). We instead operate within a single OALM, where Forced-AR, CF, and random orders are decoding choices on the same network, isolating the effect of the path π\pi from that of the parameters θ\theta.

Order-aware training and ARMD-style hybrids.

A complementary line of work modifies training so that the model better matches a chosen inference order: training on the worst-case position (11), ARMD-style training that bridges AR and any-order objectives (10), and DCD-style denoising-curriculum training (22). These methods change pθp_{\theta}, while our experiments hold pθp_{\theta} fixed and vary only the inference-side path. Our contribution is therefore not a new decoding rule, but an analysis of the confidence trace induced by a fixed trained OALM, with variance serving as an order-sensitive diagnostic complementary to likelihood.

3 Theory of Uniform Spreading

This section develops the uniform-spreading theorem, which provides a principled criterion for comparing confidence profiles induced by CF, Forced-AR, and other order-dependent decoding strategies. In our dLLM instantiation of an OALM, the model is trained to predict masked tokens given arbitrary subsets of revealed positions, with each position independently masked at a uniformly sampled rate from U⁡(0,1)U(0,1) per example (15). Every mask pattern has nonzero training probability, so a single trained network is implicitly trained on every inference order, making the comparison of decoding orders within one model meaningful. dLLMs further use block-causal attention: at any position, the model attends bidirectionally to all tokens within the same block (including mask tokens) and causally to all preceding blocks, and in the semi-autoregressive block format blocks are processed strictly left-to-right so that reveal-order strategies choose only the order of positions inside the current block. Consequently, Forced-AR decoding on a dLLM is not equivalent to a true causal AR model, which strictly masks all future positions. All theory and empirical claims about π\pi should therefore be read as claims about within-block reveal orders, not about arbitrary global permutations of the nn target positions. The main text further restricts to the one-token-per-step setting, in which π\pi reveals exactly one position per forward pass.

3.1 Decoding Decomposition

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be the vocabulary and cc the prompt context. A decoding policy π\pi selects at each step tt a position π⁡(t)\pi(t) to unmask given the revealed set Rt−1R_{t-1}. Fix a target sequence 𝐱∗=(x1∗,…,xn∗)∈𝒱n\mathbf{x}^{*}=(x^{*}_{1},\ldots,x^{*}_{n})\in\mathcal{V}^{n} conditioned on context cc. If the conditionals {pθ(⋅∣Rt−1,c)}\{p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid R_{t-1},c)\} arise from a single coherent joint distribution pp over 𝐱\mathbf{x} given cc, with P≜p⁡(𝐱∗∣c)P\triangleq p(\mathbf{x}^{*}\mid c), then the chain rule of pp guarantees that for any policy π\pi,

∏t=1nqt​(π)=P,qt​(π)≜p⁡(xπ⁡(t)∗∣Rt−1,c),\prod_{t=1}^{n}q_{t}(\pi)=P,\qquad q_{t}(\pi)\triangleq p\!\left(x^{*}_{\pi(t)}\mid R_{t-1},c\right), (1)

so the product is order-invariant while the distribution of {qt}\{q_{t}\} across steps is not. For the trained pθp_{\theta}, however, the conditionals need not arise from any single joint, so ∏tqt​(π)\prod_{t}q_{t}(\pi) may itself depend on π\pi.

To isolate the allocation question from the coherence question, we analytically hold PP fixed and ask how the per-step profile {qt​(π)}\{q_{t}(\pi)\} affects the target recoverability A⁡(π)A(\pi)—the probability that the decoder recovers the entire target 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*}. For greedy decoding at step tt, the decoder commits to arg⁡maxv​pθ​(v∣Rt−1,c)\arg\max_{v}p_{\theta}(v\mid R_{t-1},c), so the target is recovered only when it attains this argmax; this requires qtq_{t} to exceed every competitor, and the outcome therefore depends on how the residual mass 1−qt1-q_{t} is distributed among competitor tokens. Let f⁡(qt)f(q_{t}) denote the probability that greedy recovers the target at step tt; under a standard modeling assumption on the competitor distribution (deferred to App. A.1), this probability depends on the conditional distribution only through qtq_{t}. Under independence of greedy success across steps (App. A.1), A⁡(π)A(\pi) factorizes as

A⁡(π)=∏t=1nf⁡(qt​(π))=∏t=1nqt​(π)⏟=P​(order-invariant)⋅∏t=1nf⁡(qt)qt⏟D⁡(π)​(order-dependent),A(\pi)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}f\!\bigl(q_{t}(\pi)\bigr)=\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{n}q_{t}(\pi)}_{=P\;\text{(order-invariant)}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{n}\frac{f(q_{t})}{q_{t}}}_{D(\pi)\;\text{(order-dependent)}}, (2)

so all order-dependence in A⁡(π)A(\pi) is carried by the distortion D⁡(π)D(\pi).

Since PP is fixed, maximizing A⁡(π)A(\pi) reduces to maximizing D⁡(π)D(\pi) under the constraint ∏tqt=P\prod_{t}q_{t}=P, i.e. maximizing ∑tlog⁡f⁡(qt)\sum_{t}\log f(q_{t}) with ∑tlog⁡qt\sum_{t}\log q_{t} held fixed. The key analytic property that makes this tractable is that log⁡f⁡(ey)\log f(e^{y}) is strictly concave in y=log⁡qy=\log q; see App. A.4 for the proof.

3.2 Uniform Spreading

Theorem 3.1 (Uniform Spreading).

If the log-recoverability is strictly concave with respect to the log-probability, then among all step distributions (q1,…,qn)(q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}) satisfying ∏tqt=P\prod_{t}q_{t}=P, the target recoverability A=∏tf⁡(qt)A=\prod_{t}f(q_{t}) is uniquely maximized when confidence is spread uniformly across all steps:

q1=q2=⋯=qn=P1/n.q_{1}=q_{2}=\cdots=q_{n}=P^{1/n}.
Proof sketch.

Let yt=log⁡qty_{t}=\log q_{t} and L=log⁡PL=\log P. The constraint is ∑tyt=L\sum_{t}y_{t}=L, and our goal is to maximize log⁡A=∑tlog⁡f⁡(eyt)\log A=\sum_{t}\log f(e^{y_{t}}). By the concavity condition above, Jensen’s inequality gives

1n​∑t=1nlog⁡f⁡(eyt)≤log⁡f⁡(exp⁡(1n​∑t=1nyt))=log⁡f⁡(P1/n),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\log f(e^{y_{t}})\;\leq\;\log f\!\left(\exp\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}y_{t}\right)\right)=\log f\!\left(P^{1/n}\right),

with equality if and only if y1=⋯=yny_{1}=\cdots=y_{n}, yielding the upper bound A≤f​(P1/n)nA\leq f(P^{1/n})^{n} on every per-step profile. A complete proof, including the uniqueness of the maximizer, is given in App. A.5. ∎

The theorem fixes the sequence likelihood PP and isolates the effect of the per-step profile {qt}\{q_{t}\} on decoding recoverability. The intuition relies on the decoding bottleneck: because ff is nonlinear, a single low-confidence step damages the target recoverability AA super-linearly. Thus, for a given total log-probability log⁡P\log P, the optimal strategy penalizes variance and uniformly distributes the task difficulty. The theorem deliberately begins with the simplified case where the total target likelihood PP is fixed: if reveal-order imbalance can affect recoverability even there, then variance becomes even more important in the trained model, where the effective likelihood may itself vary with order.

This theoretical optimum motivates the two scalar diagnostics we use to evaluate strategies in §4: the mean log-confidence log⁡q¯:=1n​∑tlog⁡qt\overline{\log q}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{t}\log q_{t}, which measures the average self-rated difficulty along the path, and the log-probability variance Varπ:=1n​∑t(log⁡qt−log⁡q¯)2\mathrm{Var}_{\pi}:=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{t}(\log q_{t}-\overline{\log q})^{2}, which measures deviation from the uniform optimum. Theorem 3.1 predicts that, when paths have comparable log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, lower Varπ\mathrm{Var}_{\pi} should imply higher recoverability.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup and Strategies

All experiments use LLaDA-2.1-mini (3) with block size 3232 under the one-token-per-step setting of §3, so each block takes 3232 reveal steps. The strategy set separates practical decoders from diagnostic controls. The practical decoders are:

  • •

    Forced-AR: reveal positions left-to-right within each block.

  • •

    Max-prob (CF): for each unrevealed position jj in the current block, compute its score sj=maxv∈𝒱⁡pθ​(v∣Rt−1)s_{j}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta}(v\mid R_{t-1}), i.e. the largest probability assigned to any vocabulary token at position jj; reveal the position with the largest sjs_{j}.

  • •

    Top-margin (CF): for each unrevealed position jj, score it by the gap between the top two tokens of the current conditional at jj, sj=pθ​(v1∣Rt−1)−pθ​(v2∣Rt−1)s_{j}=p_{\theta}(v_{1}\mid R_{t-1})-p_{\theta}(v_{2}\mid R_{t-1}), where v1,v2∈𝒱v_{1},v_{2}\in\mathcal{V} are those top two tokens; reveal the position with the largest sjs_{j}.

Two deployable controls isolate order effects:

  • •

    Random: reveal a uniformly random unrevealed position at each step; the random seed is fixed across runs.

  • •

    Reverse-AR: reveal positions right-to-left within each block, testing whether the left-to-right direction itself explains the observed behavior.

For the fixed-sequence experiment only, we additionally use three target-aware oracle orderings. Each scores the unrevealed position jj by a target-dependent criterion and reveals the position with the largest score:

  • •

    Oracle max-qq: score position jj by the model’s probability of the target token there, sj=qj:=pθ​(xj∗∣Rt−1)s_{j}=q_{j}:=p_{\theta}(x_{j}^{*}\mid R_{t-1}); reveal the most confident target position first.

  • •

    Oracle margin: score position jj by the gap between the target probability and its largest competitor, sj=pθ​(xj∗∣Rt−1)−maxv∈𝒱,v≠xj∗⁡pθ​(v∣Rt−1)s_{j}=p_{\theta}(x_{j}^{*}\mid R_{t-1})-\max_{v\in\mathcal{V},\,v\neq x_{j}^{*}}p_{\theta}(v\mid R_{t-1}); reveal the position where the target most decisively beats its strongest competitor.

  • •

    Oracle min-qq: score position jj by sj=−qjs_{j}=-q_{j}, i.e. reveal the least confident target position first.

Oracle max-qq and Oracle margin are the target-aware counterparts of the practical CF rules Max-prob and Top-margin (replacing argmax-based scores with target-based ones), while Oracle min-qq is the opposite ordering to Oracle max-qq and acts as a lower-bound control. These oracle orderings are diagnostic rather than deployable because they require the known target 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*}; “Oracle” refers to knowledge of 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*}, not access to pp, and probabilities are still computed by pθp_{\theta}.

Datasets and protocol.

The main C4 experiments use a fixed evaluation subset of 1,0001{,}000 examples selected from the C4 validation split (19). Each example is tokenized into a 3232-token prefix followed by a 128128-token region, corresponding to four blocks and 128128 reveal steps under the one-token-per-step setting. The fixed-sequence validation (§4.2) treats this region as the held-out target and evaluates order-dependent likelihood traces. Open-ended generation (§4.3) and the unmask-order analysis (§4.3) reuse the same prefixes but let the model generate its own 128128-token continuation. Downstream evaluation (§4.4) uses the same decoding implementation on HellaSwag (30), CMath (27), MMLU-Pro (25), and IFEval (33), with task-specific prompt lengths and stopping rules detailed in App. B.

Metrics.

The two theory metrics from §3 are log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} and Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q), where qtq_{t} is the probability assigned at the revealed position to the target token (fixed-sequence scoring) or to the selected token (generation); in generation we also report their content-only variants, which exclude EOS tokens. Output-quality metrics are EOS% (fraction of generated EOS tokens), External PPL (GPT-2 Large (18)), and Distinct-3 (fraction of unique trigrams (13)). The fixed-sequence validation additionally reports single-step argmax accuracy and a Gini-style concentration coefficient over per-step within-block self-information as auxiliary statistics.

4.2 Uniform-Spreading Validation: Oracle Orderings on Fixed Sequences

We first test the two diagnostics motivated by Theorem 3.1 in a controlled setting where the 128128-token continuation of each C4 example is held fixed as the target 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} rather than generated (Fig. 1). Knowing 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} lets us evaluate the target-aware oracle orderings of §4.1 alongside the three non-CF baselines (Forced-AR, Reverse-AR, Random); all statistics are computed per sequence and averaged over the 1,0001{,}000 examples.

Finding 1: the learned conditionals are not order-coherent.

A coherent joint p∗p^{*} would, by the chain rule, give the same total log-likelihood log⁡P=∑tlog⁡p∗​(xπ⁡(t)∗∣Rt−1)\log P=\sum_{t}\log p^{*}(x^{*}_{\pi(t)}\mid R_{t-1}) for every reveal order π\pi. In practice log⁡P/n\log P/n ranges from −3.00-3.00 (Forced-AR) to −3.49-3.49 (Oracle min-qq), a ∼0.5\sim 0.5-nat-per-token spread (Fig. 1a). Thus pθ(⋅∣Rt−1)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid R_{t-1}) depends materially on the path, and log⁡P\log P alone is not order-invariant at the resolution needed for strategy comparison.

Finding 2: Varπ\mathrm{Var}_{\pi} is a non-redundant axis driven by bottleneck steps.

Across the six strategies in Fig. 1a, Varπ\mathrm{Var}_{\pi} is correlated with log⁡P/n\log P/n (Spearman ρ≈−0.77\rho\approx-0.77) but not collinear with it, and there are non-monotone pairs such as Forced-AR vs. Oracle max-qq (nearly identical log⁡P/n\log P/n, Var differs by ∼⁣×\sim\!2\!\times) and Random vs. Reverse-AR (Var ranked oppositely to log⁡P/n\log P/n). The mechanism behind this extra axis is visible in Fig. 1b: high-variance orderings push the within-block Lorenz curve farther below the uniform diagonal, i.e. self-information is concentrated in a few bottleneck steps rather than spread evenly. We therefore report both: log⁡P\log P captures the path’s absolute model confidence, while Varπ\mathrm{Var}_{\pi} captures the severity of bottleneck steps along the path.

4.3 Structured Strategies Traverse Near-Identical Reveal Orders

We now drop the ground-truth assumption: each strategy decodes its own continuation from a prompt, so the per-step qtq_{t} is the model’s own argmax probability rather than the probability assigned to a known x∗x^{*}. This removes the oracle strategies from the testable set but adds two things the fixed-sequence regime cannot offer: (i) an open-ended generation distribution, which matches practical deployment; (ii) downstream-quality measurements (external perplexity, Distinct-3, EOS%) that are only defined when the model produces text.

Finding 1: on content tokens, structured strategies reduce to near-L2R reveal paths.

On block 00, after excluding EOS reveals, the Spearman rank correlation with strict L2R is 89.1%89.1\% for Max-prob and 80.7%80.7\% for Top-margin. The two adaptive confidence-first rules therefore traverse content paths close to L2R, so the three structured orderings see nearly the same sequence of contexts {Rt−1}\{R_{t-1}\} at reveal time and consequently cluster together on log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q), and external quality in Table 1; Random, whose path has no L2R structure, is the outlier on every metric. Panels (a) and (d) of Fig. 2 illustrate this regime: panel (a) is a near-pure L2R trace with every step advancing the rightward frontier, and panel (d) is an all-content trace where Max-prob permutes only a few adjacent positions (local swaps among competing high-confidence neighbors) without disturbing the global rank order—consistent with the high but sub-unity content Spearman. The underlying driver is locality: the position immediately right of the prompt boundary has the strongest mutual information with the revealed context (d=1d{=}1 neighbor), so confidence-first decoding tends to begin there and expand rightward.

Finding 2: confidence-first strategies pre-seal the EOS tail once the answer’s right boundary becomes certain.

Once EOS tokens are included, the picture diverges: the EOS fraction in Table 1 is 2.4%2.4\% for Forced-AR but 7.9%7.9\% and 11.9%11.9\% for Max-prob and Top-margin. The mechanism is visible in Fig. 2(b,c): the model becomes confident about where the generation should end before it has finished writing the answer, so EOS has non-trivial probability at the rightmost tail positions while interior content is still masked. Forced-AR, bound to strict L2R, never exploits this; confidence-first rules open the tail. In panel (b) only three content tokens are revealed L2R before, at step 44, the rightmost position commits to EOS at 0.500.50 confidence, after which its neighbors activate as high-confidence EOS (0.850.85–0.970.97) and seventeen tail positions seal right-to-left in one cascade; only at step 2222 does decoding return to the middle. Panel (c) is a milder variant, with tail EOS committed before the answer is fully written but interleaved with content infill. Both are driven by the same trigger—growing certainty about the right boundary outweighing remaining content confidence—but differ only in when and how sharply it fires. The content Spearman of Finding 1 excludes EOS precisely to factor out this effect, which is why the content metric stays close to 11 across all four panels despite visibly different EOS timing.

4.4 Downstream Tasks: Reasoning, Math, and Instruction Following

Theorem 3.1 does not directly prove task accuracy; rather, it motivates uneven confidence profiles as a diagnostic of bottlenecked decoding trajectories. We next test whether this diagnostic transfers to externally graded correctness on standard benchmarks, where each generation receives a binary label rather than a self-reported likelihood. We run the four pure one-token-per-step orderings on four benchmarks and log the per-token log-probability of every revealed token along the way.

Setup.

We use the same LLaDA-2.1-mini checkpoint and one-token-per-step decoding implementation as above, with EOS early stopping and no correction procedure. The reveal order is the only factor varied across cells. For every revealed token we log (position,token id,log⁡qt)(\text{position},\,\text{token id},\,\log q_{t}), where qt=pθ​(x^t∣Rt−1)q_{t}=p_{\theta}(\hat{x}_{t}\mid R_{t-1}) is the model’s confidence in its own selected token at reveal time. EOS tokens are excluded from log-probability statistics; further decoding details are in App. B. HellaSwag (30) (N=10,042N{=}10{,}042, validation set; commonsense 4-way MCQ); CMath (27) (N=1,098N{=}1{,}098, test split; Chinese primary-school arithmetic word problems); MMLU-Pro (25) (N=12,032N{=}12{,}032, test split; 10-way reasoning-heavy MCQ); IFEval (33) (N=541N{=}541; rule-based instruction following with both prompt-strict and instruction-strict accuracies). All four strategies see the same prompts.

Finding 1: structured paths form a low-variance, higher-accuracy tier.

Table 2 shows the same tiering as the C4 experiments: Random has the lowest accuracy and the highest content Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) on every benchmark, while the three structured strategies cluster within ±1.6\pm 1.6 pp with no stable winner inside the low-Var tier. This matches Theorem 3.1: the prediction is the separation between high-Var and low-Var paths, not an ordering among near-overlapping structured ones. Using content Var\mathrm{Var} as a prompt-level selector (argmin-Var) matches the best single fixed strategy to within ∼2{\sim}2 pp on all four benchmarks and consistently exceeds the argmax-Var selector by Δ=+2.9\Delta=+2.9 to +32.8+32.8 pp: the low-variance path positively predicts correctness relative to the high-variance one.

Finding 2: the Var\mathrm{Var}–correctness link is not driven by strategy-level effects.

To rule out that the pooled association is driven by Random alone, we restrict to the 4×4=164\times 4=16 (benchmark, strategy) cells (Table 3), in each of which both benchmark and strategy are held fixed. Correct samples have strictly lower mean Var\mathrm{Var} than incorrect ones in all 1616 cells, with the one-sided Mann–Whitney UU test highly significant in most cells; the per-cell Spearman ρ⁡(Var, 1correct)\rho(\mathrm{Var},\,\mathbf{1}_{\text{correct}}) is negative in every cell, including the structured-only ones. Thus Var\mathrm{Var} genuinely tracks correctness rather than reflecting a strategy-level outlier.

Finding 3: mean confidence and variance are complementary axes.

We next ask whether the Var signal is already captured by the classical log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}. Splitting samples within each benchmark by median content log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} and median content Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) yields four quadrants (Table 4). At matched log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, low-Var\mathrm{Var} is never worse than high-Var\mathrm{Var}. CMath is especially striking: the lo-log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}/lo-Var quadrant reaches 94.1%94.1\%, above the hi-log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}/hi-Var quadrant at 89.6%89.6\%—a low-confidence but low-variance generation is more reliable than a high-confidence but high-variance one, indicating that in some regimes Var\mathrm{Var} carries signal beyond log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}. We therefore recommend reporting log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} and Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) jointly rather than collapsing them into a single scalar.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

On the trained OALM studied here, log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} is not order-invariant: the ∼0.5{\sim}0.5-nat/token chain-rule deviation in LLaDA-2.1-mini is far above numerical tolerance, so mean confidence alone mixes content difficulty with the ordering of easy and hard positions. On natural language, the structured strategies (Forced-AR, Max-prob, Top-margin) trace near-identical content reveal paths while Random forms the high-variance, lower-quality tier; on short-answer prompts, confidence-first rules additionally trigger a tail-EOS cascade that Forced-AR cannot exploit (§4.3). Theorem 3.1 supplies the order-dependent complement Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}): even at fixed confidence budget, bottlenecked traces are less recoverable than uniformly spread ones—a minimal fixed-PP case, since the trained model is more complex with ∏tqt​(π)\prod_{t}q_{t}(\pi) also order-dependent. Variance is thus not a substitute for accuracy or likelihood but a supplementary diagnostic for whether a path is stable or driven by bottlenecked, order-sensitive steps. The downstream results are consistent with this diagnostic view: low-variance paths form the higher-accuracy tier, and the Var–correctness association survives after fixing both benchmark and strategy (§4.4). We therefore read (log⁡q¯,Var⁡(log⁡q))(\overline{\log q},\mathrm{Var}(\log q)) as a joint diagnostic plane: low log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} + high Var = poor and unstable; high log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} + high Var = average confidence driven by a few favorable steps; similar log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} but lower Var = the more stable order or policy. We recommend reporting them jointly. The primary strategy-level distinction we observe is between structured low-variance paths and Random; restoring chain-rule coherence is a training-side problem outside our scope.

6 Limitations

(i) While we use dLLMs as a representative OALM testbed, all experiments rely on one checkpoint and scale (LLaDA-2.1-mini); transfer to larger LLaDA variants and other architectures (MDLM, SEDD, XLNet) remains open. The proposed joint reporting of log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} and Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) is model-agnostic, but the empirical rankings should be interpreted at this scale. (ii) The main experiments focus on one-token-per-step decoding. Parallel decoding, where multiple tokens are committed simultaneously, introduces a separate batch-coupling effect; extending the variance diagnostic to jointly account for order and batch size is left for future work. (iii) Our variance analysis is diagnostic rather than a new deployable decoding algorithm. The prompt-level min-V selector uses logged trajectories to test whether low variance predicts correctness; designing an online policy that reduces variance without oracle comparisons is a separate problem.

Appendix A Proofs and Derivations

A.1 Setup: Chain Rule and Distortion Decomposition

Notation.

The prompt or context is denoted by cc, the target sequence by 𝐱∗=(x1∗,…,xn∗)\mathbf{x}^{*}=(x_{1}^{*},\ldots,x_{n}^{*}), and the reveal order by π\pi, where π⁡(t)\pi(t) is the position revealed at step tt. The set of already revealed tokens before step tt is Rt−1R_{t-1}. We write qtq_{t} for the model probability assigned to the target token xπ⁡(t)∗x^{*}_{\pi(t)} at that step, and P=p⁡(𝐱∗∣c)P=p(\mathbf{x}^{*}\mid c) for the reference sequence probability. The vocabulary is 𝒱\mathcal{V} with size S=|𝒱|S=|\mathcal{V}|; for LLaDA-2.1-mini, S=32,000S=32{,}000. All logarithms are natural logarithms.

Chain-rule baseline.

If the conditionals came from a coherent joint distribution p⁡(𝐱∣c)p(\mathbf{x}\mid c), then for any reveal order π\pi,

∏t=1nqt​(π)=P,qt​(π)=p⁡(xπ⁡(t)∗∣Rt−1,c),P=p⁡(𝐱∗∣c).\prod_{t=1}^{n}q_{t}(\pi)=P,\qquad q_{t}(\pi)=p\!\left(x^{*}_{\pi(t)}\mid R_{t-1},c\right),\qquad P=p(\mathbf{x}^{*}\mid c).

The product is independent of the order. Empirically, however, LLaDA-2.1 changes log⁡P/n\log P/n by up to 0.490.49 nats/token across reveal orders, so the learned conditionals should not be treated as exact factorizations of one joint distribution. We therefore use the chain-rule identity as an analytic reference point and separately track order-sensitive diagnostics.

Greedy decoding and distortion.

Greedy decoding succeeds at step tt only if the target token wins the local argmax. Let f⁡(qt)f(q_{t}) denote the probability that this step recovers the target token when the model assigns target probability qtq_{t}. The effective sequence recovery probability is

A⁡(π)=∏t=1nf⁡(qt).A(\pi)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}f(q_{t}).

Multiplying and dividing by the chain-rule product isolates the order-dependent part:

A⁡(π)=∏t=1nf⁡(qt)=∏t=1nqt⏟=P​(order-invariant reference)​∏t=1nf⁡(qt)qt⏟D⁡(π)​(order-dependent).A(\pi)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}f(q_{t})=\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{n}q_{t}}_{=\,P\ \text{(order-invariant reference)}}\;\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{n}\frac{f(q_{t})}{q_{t}}}_{D(\pi)\ \text{(order-dependent)}}. (3)

Thus A=P⋅DA=P\cdot D. With PP fixed, maximizing AA is equivalent to maximizing the distortion term D⁡(π)D(\pi).

Independence clarification.

The product form A⁡(π)=∏tf⁡(qt)A(\pi)=\prod_{t}f(q_{t}) is a conditional step-success model: at step tt, the success probability is evaluated conditioned on all previously revealed tokens being correct. The random logit noises ϵv(t)\epsilon_{v}^{(t)} are taken independent across steps in this model, while the confidences qtq_{t} themselves need not be independent because they are determined by the revealed context Rt−1R_{t-1}. Thus the factorization concerns the noise variables used to model local greedy decisions, not independence of the confidence trace.

A.2 Explicit Greedy-Success Function

We next derive the one-step success probability f⁡(q)f(q) under the single-competitor Gaussian-logit model used in the proof. Let q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) be the model probability assigned to the target token. Greedy decoding assigns each token a noisy logit

ℓv=log⁡pv+ϵv,ϵv​∼iid​𝒩​(0,σ2),\ell_{v}=\log p_{v}+\epsilon_{v},\qquad\epsilon_{v}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),

and selects the largest logit. The target must beat every other token; equivalently, it must beat the strongest competitor, or runner-up. We therefore model this binding competitor directly: the target has probability qq, and the runner-up carries the residual mass 1−q1-q. Concentrating the residual mass on one competitor is the hardest single-competitor allocation for the target to beat, so the resulting ff is a conservative one-step success model. This gives the two logits

ℓtarget=log⁡q+ϵtarget,ℓcomp=log⁡(1−q)+ϵcomp.\ell_{\mathrm{target}}=\log q+\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}},\qquad\ell_{\mathrm{comp}}=\log(1-q)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}.

The target is selected iff

ℓtarget>ℓcomp⟺Δ≜ϵcomp−ϵtarget<logq−log(1−q).\ell_{\mathrm{target}}>\ell_{\mathrm{comp}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta\triangleq\epsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}-\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}}<\log q-\log(1-q).

Since Δ∼𝒩⁡(0,2​σ2)\Delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2\sigma^{2}), standardizing by its standard deviation σ​2\sigma\sqrt{2} yields

f(q)=Pr[Δ<logq−log(1−q)]=Φ(log⁡q−log⁡(1−q)σ​2).f(q)=\Pr\!\left[\Delta<\log q-\log(1-q)\right]=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log q-\log(1-q)}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}\right). (4)

Now set y=log⁡qy=\log q and define the standardized margin

z⁡(y)=log⁡q−log⁡(1−q)σ​2=y−log⁡(1−ey)σ​2.z(y)=\frac{\log q-\log(1-q)}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}=\frac{y-\log(1-e^{y})}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}. (5)

Then

f⁡(q)=Φ⁡(z⁡(y))\boxed{\;f(q)=\Phi(z(y))\;}

where Φ\Phi is the standard-normal CDF,

Φ(a)=Pr[Z≤a]=∫−∞a12​πe−u2/2du,Z∼𝒩(0,1).\Phi(a)=\Pr[Z\leq a]=\int_{-\infty}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^{2}/2}\,du,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

The argument z⁡(y)z(y) is a standardized margin: its numerator is the target-vs-competitor log-probability gap, and its denominator σ​2\sigma\sqrt{2} is the standard deviation of the noise difference. Thus f⁡(q)=Φ⁡(z⁡(y))f(q)=\Phi(z(y)) is the probability that the target beats the runner-up. This single-competitor expression is exact for the two-token comparison and does not depend on the vocabulary size. For greedy decoding, this is the per-step success probability used in the distortion decomposition, so h=fh=f.

A.3 Log-Space Objective

Jensen’s inequality applies after converting the multiplicative constraint into a sum. Let

yt=log⁡qt,L=log⁡P.y_{t}=\log q_{t},\qquad L=\log P.

Then ∏tqt=P\prod_{t}q_{t}=P becomes

∑t=1nyt=L.\sum_{t=1}^{n}y_{t}=L.

Define the log-recoverability function

g⁡(y)≜log⁡f⁡(ey)=(log⁡Φ)​(z⁡(y)).g(y)\triangleq\log f(e^{y})=(\log\Phi)(z(y)). (6)

The sequence log-recovery probability is therefore

log⁡A=∑tlog⁡f⁡(qt)=∑tg⁡(yt).\log A=\sum_{t}\log f(q_{t})=\sum_{t}g(y_{t}).

The relevant concavity is concavity of gg as a function of y=log⁡qy=\log q, not concavity of ff as a function of qq.

In the outer-derivative calculation below, zz denotes a generic real argument of log⁡Φ\log\Phi; after those derivatives are computed, we substitute back z=z⁡(y)z=z(y).

g′′​(y)=−r⁡(z)​(z+r⁡(z))​[z′​(y)]2+r⁡(z)​z′′​(y).g^{\prime\prime}(y)=-r(z)\bigl(z+r(z)\bigr)[z^{\prime}(y)]^{2}+r(z)z^{\prime\prime}(y).

g′′​(y)=r⁡(z)​[z′′​(y)−(z+r⁡(z))​[z′​(y)]2].\boxed{\;g^{\prime\prime}(y)=r(z)\Bigl[z^{\prime\prime}(y)-\bigl(z+r(z)\bigr)[z^{\prime}(y)]^{2}\Bigr].\;} (8)

Step 5: reduce to a scalar criterion.

Since r⁡(z)>0r(z)>0, the sign of g′′g^{\prime\prime} is the sign of the bracket in (8). The condition g′′​(y)<0g^{\prime\prime}(y)<0 is equivalent to

(z+r⁡(z))​[z′​(y)]2>z′′​(y).\bigl(z+r(z)\bigr)[z^{\prime}(y)]^{2}>z^{\prime\prime}(y).

Substituting the expressions for z′z^{\prime} and z′′z^{\prime\prime}, and writing q=eyq=e^{y}, gives

z+r⁡(z)2​σ2​(1−q)2>qσ​2​(1−q)2⟺z+r⁡(z)2​σ2>qσ​2⟺z+r(z)>2σq.\frac{z+r(z)}{2\sigma^{2}(1-q)^{2}}>\frac{q}{\sigma\sqrt{2}(1-q)^{2}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{z+r(z)}{2\sigma^{2}}>\frac{q}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z+r(z)>\sqrt{2}\,\sigma q.

Thus

g′′(y)<0⟺z(q)+r(z(q))>2σq,z(q)=log⁡q−log⁡(1−q)σ​2.\boxed{\;g^{\prime\prime}(y)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z(q)+r\!\bigl(z(q)\bigr)>\sqrt{2}\,\sigma q,\qquad z(q)=\frac{\log q-\log(1-q)}{\sigma\sqrt{2}}.\;} (9)

This criterion is the useful point. The left-hand side z+r⁡(z)z+r(z) is always positive by the Mills-ratio argument above, while the right-hand side 2​σ​q\sqrt{2}\,\sigma q scales linearly with the noise level. The sign is therefore controlled by σ\sigma, not by a separate assumption that q≪1q\ll 1: as q→0q\to 0 the right-hand side also vanishes, and moderate or large values of qq can still satisfy the criterion when σ\sigma is small.

Step 6: small-σ\sigma sign.

The noise scale σ\sigma is the smoothing parameter that turns the deterministic argmax event into the smooth probability Φ⁡(z)\Phi(z); in the zero-noise limit this recovers the hard threshold 𝟏[q>12]\mathbf{1}[q>\tfrac{1}{2}]. It is therefore natural to analyze the σ→0\sigma\to 0 regime. Let s=σ​2s=\sigma\sqrt{2} and z=logit⁡(q)/sz=\mathrm{logit}(q)/s. We show that for sufficiently small σ\sigma, the criterion (9) holds for all q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1).

If q≥12q\geq\tfrac{1}{2}, then z≥0z\geq 0 and z+r⁡(z)≥r⁡(0)=2/πz+r(z)\geq r(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}. Also 2​σ​q=s​q<s\sqrt{2}\,\sigma q=sq<s, so the criterion holds whenever σ≤1/π\sigma\leq 1/\sqrt{\pi}.

If q<12q<\tfrac{1}{2}, then z→−∞z\to-\infty as σ→0\sigma\to 0. Mills’ expansion gives

z+r⁡(z)=−1z+O⁡(z−3)=s|logit⁡(q)|+O⁡(s3)=σ​2|logit⁡(q)|+O⁡(σ3).z+r(z)=-\frac{1}{z}+O(z^{-3})=\frac{s}{|\mathrm{logit}(q)|}+O(s^{3})=\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2}}{|\mathrm{logit}(q)|}+O(\sigma^{3}).

Therefore

z+r⁡(z)−2​σ​q=σ​2|logit⁡(q)|​(1−q​|logit⁡(q)|)+O⁡(σ3).z+r(z)-\sqrt{2}\,\sigma q=\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2}}{|\mathrm{logit}(q)|}\Bigl(1-q|\mathrm{logit}(q)|\Bigr)+O(\sigma^{3}).

Since

maxq∈(0,1/2)⁡q​|logit⁡(q)|≈0.2785<1,\max_{q\in(0,1/2)}q|\mathrm{logit}(q)|\approx 0.2785<1,

with the maximum attained near q≈0.218q\approx 0.218, the factor 1−q​|logit⁡(q)|1-q|\mathrm{logit}(q)| is bounded below by approximately 0.7215>00.7215>0. Hence the leading term is positive, and the criterion holds for sufficiently small σ\sigma in this case as well.

Combining both cases,

∃σ0>0:∀σ≤σ0,∀q∈(0,1),g′′(y)<0.\boxed{\;\exists\,\sigma_{0}>0:\ \forall\,\sigma\leq\sigma_{0},\ \forall\,q\in(0,1),\quad g^{\prime\prime}(y)<0.\;}

Numerically, the admissible range extends to approximately σ0≈1.05\sigma_{0}\approx 1.05; at σ=0.1\sigma=0.1, the swept margin z+r−2​σ​qz+r-\sqrt{2}\sigma q remains positive over q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). ∎

Extension to multiple competitors.

For kk competitors, let ϵ0\epsilon_{0} be the target noise and ϵ1,…,ϵk\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{k} the competitor noises. Define

Wk≜maxi=1,…,k(ϵi−ϵ0),FWk(w)=Pr[Wk≤w].W_{k}\triangleq\max_{i=1,\ldots,k}(\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{0}),\qquad F_{W_{k}}(w)=\Pr[W_{k}\leq w].

If the residual mass 1−q1-q is spread uniformly over kk competitors, the one-step success probability is

fk​(q)=FWk​(log⁡k​q1−q),f_{k}(q)=F_{W_{k}}\!\left(\log\frac{kq}{1-q}\right),

where (ϵ1−ϵ0,…,ϵk−ϵ0)(\epsilon_{1}-\epsilon_{0},\ldots,\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{0}) is a mean-zero multivariate Gaussian with covariance σ2​(I+𝟏𝟏⊤)\sigma^{2}(I+\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}). For k=1k=1, W1∼𝒩⁡(0,2​σ2)W_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2\sigma^{2}) and this reduces to (4). For k≥2k\geq 2, FWkF_{W_{k}} has no elementary closed form, but w↦log⁡FWk​(w)w\mapsto\log F_{W_{k}}(w) is concave by Prékopa’s theorem (17). Applying the same two-term decomposition as above gives the same mechanism. The two extremes are k=1k=1 (a single dominant competitor) and k=S−1k=S-1 (residual mass spread over all non-target vocabulary items); in realistic softmax distributions, only a small effective set of competitors usually carries substantial mass, so the regime lies between these extremes. Numerical checks with Zipfian competitor masses preserve the sign in the regime used here. Thus the competitor distribution mainly changes the effective noise scale; the single-competitor model is a clean base case rather than a load-bearing vocabulary-size assumption.

A.5 Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Uniform Spreading)

Proof.

We maximize

log⁡A=∑t=1ng⁡(yt)subject to∑t=1nyt=L.\log A=\sum_{t=1}^{n}g(y_{t})\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{n}y_{t}=L.

Since gg is concave by App. A.4, Jensen’s inequality gives

1n​∑t=1ng⁡(yt)≤g⁡(1n​∑t=1nyt)=g⁡(Ln).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}g(y_{t})\leq g\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}y_{t}\right)=g\!\left(\frac{L}{n}\right).

Equality holds iff y1=⋯=yn=L/ny_{1}=\cdots=y_{n}=L/n, equivalently

q1=q2=⋯=qn=P1/n.\boxed{\;q_{1}=q_{2}=\cdots=q_{n}=P^{1/n}\;}.

At this point AA takes the value [f⁡(P1/n)]n[f(P^{1/n})]^{n}.

For uniqueness, equivalently form the Lagrangian

J=∑tg⁡(yt)−λ⁡(∑tyt−L).J=\sum_{t}g(y_{t})-\lambda\left(\sum_{t}y_{t}-L\right).

The stationarity condition is g′​(yt)=λg^{\prime}(y_{t})=\lambda for all tt. Strict concavity makes g′g^{\prime} strictly decreasing and therefore one-to-one, so all yty_{t} must be equal. Concavity then makes this stationary point the global maximizer. ∎

Intuition.

Greedy decoding is a chain of local decisions: if one step has too little confidence and loses the local argmax, the whole target sequence fails even if other steps are easy. Under a fixed total log-probability budget, spreading difficulty evenly across steps avoids such bottlenecks. This is the same water-filling principle in another form: fixed budget plus concave per-step utility implies a uniform optimum.

Why variance is the diagnostic.

The theorem identifies the uniform point but not the local cost of moving away from it. Let

y¯=Ln=1n​∑tyt.\bar{y}=\frac{L}{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t}y_{t}.

Expanding each g⁡(yt)g(y_{t}) around y¯\bar{y} gives

g⁡(yt)≈g⁡(y¯)+g′​(y¯)​(yt−y¯)+12​g′′​(y¯)​(yt−y¯)2.g(y_{t})\approx g(\bar{y})+g^{\prime}(\bar{y})(y_{t}-\bar{y})+\frac{1}{2}g^{\prime\prime}(\bar{y})(y_{t}-\bar{y})^{2}.

Summing over tt, the linear term vanishes because ∑t(yt−y¯)=0\sum_{t}(y_{t}-\bar{y})=0, and

∑t(yt−y¯)2=n​Var​(log⁡q).\sum_{t}(y_{t}-\bar{y})^{2}=n\,\mathrm{Var}(\log q).

Therefore

log⁡A≈n​g​(y¯)⏟set by mean ​log⁡q¯−n2|g′′​(y¯)|Var⁡(log⁡q).\boxed{\;\log A\approx\underbrace{n\,g(\bar{y})}_{\text{set by mean }\overline{\log q}}-\frac{n}{2}\bigl|g^{\prime\prime}(\bar{y})\bigr|\,\mathrm{Var}(\log q).\;}

Thus, when the mean log-confidence is matched, the leading loss relative to the uniform optimum is proportional to Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q). This gives the two diagnostics used in the experiments:

log⁡q¯=1n​∑tlog⁡qt,Varπ=1n​∑t(log⁡qt−log⁡q¯)2.\overline{\log q}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t}\log q_{t},\qquad\mathrm{Var}_{\pi}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t}\left(\log q_{t}-\overline{\log q}\right)^{2}.

The prediction is that, among paths with comparable log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, lower Varπ\mathrm{Var}_{\pi} should correspond to higher recoverability. This is why the experiments report both log⁡q¯\overline{\log q} and Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) rather than collapsing the confidence trace to one scalar.

Appendix B Downstream-Evaluation Protocol and Diagnostics

This appendix details the evaluation protocol for the downstream experiments reported in §4.4 and Table 2, then gives the paired diagnostic tests behind the per-sample uniformity claims.

Benchmarks and grading.

  • •

    HellaSwag (30): validation split, 10,04210{,}042 items total. Each example presents a context plus four candidate endings; greedy CoT generation (26), then ending selected by normalized log-probability of the four candidates given the generation.

  • •

    CMath (27): full test split, n=1,098n{=}1{,}098. Chinese primary-school arithmetic word problems; the last numeric span in the generated response is extracted and compared to the reference answer (string-equality after numeric normalization).

  • •

    MMLU-Pro (25): test split, 12,03212{,}032 items. 00-shot CoT (12) with OpenCompass-aligned (16) “Answer: X” extraction (regex on the last line); 1010-way MCQ.

  • •

    IFEval (33): train split, full n=541n{=}541 prompts (834834 atomic instructions). Rule-based scorer; we report both prompt-strict (sample is correct iff every listed instruction is satisfied) and instruction-strict accuracy (instruction-level mean).

Strategies and decoding budget.

We evaluate the four pure one-token-per-step orderings of §4.3: Forced-AR, Max-prob, Top-margin, and Random, all decoded greedily (softmax temperature T=0T{=}0) with a maximum generation length of 16,38416{,}384 tokens, end-of-sequence (EOS) early-stop, and no token-correction. Same prompt formatting across all four strategies. Generation uses a block-causal KV-cached one-token-per-step driver, and all four benchmarks are run on the same LLaDA-2.1-mini checkpoint.

Per-token logging.

For every revealed token we record (position,token id,log⁡qt)(\text{position},\,\text{token id},\,\log q_{t}), where qtq_{t} is the model’s argmax probability at the time the position is committed (computed from the same forward pass that the strategy uses to choose the position). The content statistics in Table S1 (log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q), ntokn_{\text{tok}}) are computed from this per-token log after dropping EOS tokens.

Sample-size and CI.

For binary accuracy with observed proportion p^\hat{p}, the 95%95\% CI half-width 1.96​p^​(1−p^)/n1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n} is at most ±4.2\pm 4.2pp at n=541n{=}541 (IFEval), ±3.0\pm 3.0pp at n=1,098n{=}1{,}098 (CMath), ±1.0\pm 1.0pp at n=10,042n{=}10{,}042 (HellaSwag), and ±0.9\pm 0.9pp at n=12,032n{=}12{,}032 (MMLU-Pro). The Random-vs-rest gaps in Table 2 (66–3535pp) all exceed this floor by an order of magnitude on every benchmark; the within-uniformity gaps (≤1.6\leq 1.6pp on HellaSwag and IFEval) do not. The per-sample tests in Table 3 are not subject to this n\sqrt{n} floor because they are paired tests with at least 500500 samples per cell.

B.1 Downstream Diagnostic Tests

Per-cell content statistics.

Table S1 reports the per-cell content log⁡q¯\overline{\log q}, Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q), and ntokn_{\mathrm{tok}} underlying the downstream analysis in the main text. All quantities exclude EOS tokens and are averaged over the samples in the corresponding cell.

Per-cell Spearman correlations.

Table S2 reports Spearman ρ\rho between per-sample Var⁡(log⁡q)\mathrm{Var}(\log q) and the binary correctness flag; the correlation is negative in all sixteen cells (four datasets ×\times four strategies), supporting a monotonic rather than tail-driven relationship. The correlations are strongest on MMLU-Pro for the structured strategies (−0.30-0.30 to −0.34-0.34) and on CMath for Random (−0.39-0.39), and weakest on IFEval (|ρ|≤0.13|\rho|\leq 0.13). The pattern is consistent with the prediction that Var-correctness coupling tightens on benchmarks with a single-token bottleneck (MCQ >{>} math word problems >{>} free-form instruction following).

Appendix C Greedy vs. Sampling: Additional Robustness Checks

The theory and the main-text experiments are stated for greedy decoding (T=0T{=}0). Here we ask two questions. (Q1) Does sampling help? That is, for a fixed reveal-order strategy, does softmax sampling at T>0T{>}0 improve over greedy? (Q2) How does the separation of Max-prob decoding evolve under sampling? We sweep the softmax temperature T∈{0,0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0,1.3,1.5,2.0}T\in\{0,0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0,1.3,1.5,2.0\} for the four strategies Forced-AR, Max-prob, Top-margin, and Random on the open-ended generation setup of §4.3 (one-token-per-step, 1,0001{,}000 C4 prompts, generation length 128128), and report per-strategy quality including externally-graded GPT-2 Large perplexity (Ext-PPL). We report the median Ext-PPL throughout because the per-prompt PPL distribution is heavy-tailed (a small number of generations have PPL >103>10^{3} while the bulk stays below 3030).

(Q1) Greedy gives the lowest external perplexity in this sweep.

Fig. S1(a) answers (Q1) in the negative for this setting. For every reveal-order strategy, the greedy star sits at or below every point on the same-coloured sampling curve: external-perplexity medians are 7.567.56 / 7.547.54 / 7.477.47 / 11.6411.64 for Forced-AR/Max-prob/Top-margin/Random at T=0T{=}0, while the best sampling temperature for each strategy only matches (Max-prob: T=0.3T{=}0.3 gives 7.647.64) or underperforms greedy. This is consistent with Theorem 3.1: for a fixed policy π\pi, injecting multiplicative per-step noise increases Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) and hence the deviation from the uniform-spreading optimum. Panel (b) shows the same pattern: Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) increases monotonically with TT for all four strategies, with greedy giving the smallest variance.

(Q2) Sampling separates Max-prob.

At T=0T{=}0, the external-perplexity gap between Forced-AR (7.567.56), Max-prob (7.547.54), and Top-margin (7.477.47) is small; only Random (11.6411.64) is separated from the structured strategies. At T>0T{>}0, Max-prob’s external perplexity increases more slowly (7.64→7.94→8.68→10.357.64\to 7.94\to 8.68\to 10.35 at T∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0}T\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,1.0\}), while Forced-AR and Top-margin increase more rapidly (13.113.1 / 14.114.1 at T=0.7T{=}0.7; 9696 / 224224 at T=1T{=}1). Random increases earliest. The same ordering appears on the uniform-spreading probe Var⁡(log⁡qt)\mathrm{Var}(\log q_{t}) in panel (b): at T=1T{=}1, Max-prob’s within-sequence variance is 1.501.50, vs. 26.326.3 / 31.431.4 / 27.527.5 for the other three, i.e. Max-prob is ∼20×\sim 20\times more uniform under sampling noise. The cross-strategy spread on external perplexity (median max minus median min across the four strategies) grows from 4.24.2 at T=0T{=}0, to 5.15.1 at T=0.3T{=}0.3, to 20.920.9 at T=0.7T{=}0.7, to 495495 at T=1T{=}1—a ∼120×{\sim}120\times increase as we move from greedy to moderate-temperature sampling. This supports the prediction of Theorem 3.1: the noise-tolerance margin associated with uniform spreading is small when there is little sampling noise, but grows with the noise level. Thus, although greedy remains best in this sweep, Max-prob changes more slowly than the other strategies under sampling.

High-temperature regime.

At T≥1.3T{\geq}1.3 all four strategies enter a high-temperature regime: external perplexity exceeds 10310^{3} (panel (a), shaded band), content log-prob falls below −12-12 nats per token (panel (c)), and the EOS fraction drops to nearly zero because the model no longer reaches a natural stopping point within the budget (panel (d)). The shaded region in panels (a)/(b) marks this regime; we exclude it from qualitative comparisons.

Relation to the main-text downstream protocol.

The main-text downstream evaluation (§4.4) uses greedy decoding. In this sweep, greedy is the best point on the temperature curve for each reveal-order strategy, while sampling primarily enlarges the cross-strategy gap and separates Max-prob from the other strategies.

Caveat.

The temperatures here are applied uniformly across all positions; learnable position-dependent or step-dependent schedules (e.g. decreasing TT as decoding progresses) might shift the curves but should not affect the qualitative ordering predicted by the theory. External perplexity is scored by GPT-2 Large on the concatenated (prompt,gen-text)(\text{prompt},\text{gen-text}), so it reflects open-ended coherence to an AR evaluator rather than task accuracy.
